journeyIntro: For people sharing love and everyday life. Practise speaking openly, handling disagreements and staying close.

lessons.title: A Softer Start
lessons.summary: Bring up the little things without blame.

steps.title: The first line sets the tone
steps.body: How a conversation begins often decides how it ends. Open with blame and your partner is busy defending themselves before they’ve even heard the request.

steps.title: Try a soft start-up
steps.body: Say what happened, how it left you feeling and what you’d like. “The sink’s full and I’m wiped out. Could you do the dishes tonight?”

steps.prompt: Your partner has left the dinner dishes again and you’re exhausted. Which opening is most likely to get help?

options.text: “You never help with anything.”
options.why: “Never” turns one evening into a verdict on them, so they defend themselves instead of helping.

options.text: “I’m wiped out and the sink’s full. Could you take the dishes tonight?”
options.why: It names the situation and your need, and gives them something easy to say yes to.

options.text: Wash everything in silence and stew about it.
options.why: It keeps the peace tonight, but resentment builds and they have no idea anything’s wrong.

steps.prompt: Swap blame for a feeling.
steps.after: when the dishes pile up after dinner.
steps.why: It describes your state without guessing at their motives, which keeps the door open.

steps.prompt: When something small bugs you at home, what do you usually do first?
steps.reply: Knowing your habit helps you catch it next time and reach for a softer opening.

steps.prompt: Harsh start or soft start?

cards.text: “You never think about anyone but yourself.”
“I’m feeling stretched. Could we split tonight’s jobs?”
“Can I ask for something small that would really help?”

steps.why: A soft start names your feeling and asks for something specific; a harsh one attacks, and the talk goes downhill from there.

steps.body: Next time something small bothers you, start with what happened and what you’d like, not what they “always” do.

lessons.title: Complain Without Blame
lessons.summary: Name the problem, not a flaw in your partner.

steps.title: A complaint is not a criticism
steps.body: A complaint is about one situation: “The bins didn’t go out.” A criticism is about who they are: “You’re so lazy.” Complaints can be solved. Criticism just starts a defence.

steps.prompt: Your partner forgot to call the plumber again, and the sink is still leaking. Which line is a complaint, not a criticism?

options.text: “The sink’s still leaking and I’m stressed. Could you call them today?”
options.why: It names the situation, your feeling and a request, without judging their character.

options.text: “You never follow through on anything.”
options.why: “Never” and “anything” turn one slip into a verdict on who they are.

options.text: “Typical. I’ll just do it myself, like always.”
options.why: The sarcasm and “like always” add blame, so they’ll hear an attack.

steps.prompt: Swap the label for the situation.
steps.why: Naming the actual thing keeps it fixable and keeps your partner off the defensive.

steps.prompt: Which blaming word slips out most when you’re annoyed?
steps.reply: Catching that one word is often enough to turn a criticism into a complaint.

steps.prompt: Complaint or criticism?

cards.text: “I felt left out at the party.”

steps.why: Complaints describe a moment or a feeling. Criticisms describe a person, which is why they hurt and rarely change anything.

steps.body: Next time something bugs you, describe the situation and how you feel, without one word about their character.

lessons.title: Pick Your Moment
lessons.summary: The right time helps a hard talk go well.

steps.title: Timing changes everything
steps.body: The same words land very differently at 11pm, in the car with the kids, or two minutes after they walk in. Choosing a calm moment gives a tricky topic a real chance.

steps.prompt: You want to talk about spending less time with their parents. When is the best moment to raise it?

options.text: In the car on the way to their parents’ house.
options.why: They can’t really engage, and it may colour the whole visit.

options.text: Late at night, when you’re both in bed and tired.
options.why: Tired brains get defensive faster, so small talks grow big.

options.text: “Can we chat about weekends sometime this week? No rush.”
options.why: Asking for a time lets you both arrive calm and ready to listen.

steps.prompt: Ask before you start.
steps.why: A simple check gives your partner the chance to say yes when they can really listen.

steps.prompt: When do your hardest conversations usually happen?
steps.reply: Moving even one of those talks to a calmer moment can change how it goes.

steps.title: Straight through the door

lines.text: Ugh, what a day. The train was cancelled AND I missed lunch.
I just want to lie down 😩

steps.prompt: You wanted to talk holiday budget. What do you say?

options.text: Okay, but quickly, we need to sort the holiday money.
options.why: Raising it now means they’re too drained to think it through.

options.text: Oh no, sounds awful. Go and lie down. Can we look at holiday plans tomorrow evening?
options.why: You meet their needs now and book a better time for the talk.

options.text: Fine. I’ll just decide the budget myself then.
options.why: It turns their bad day into a new conflict.

steps.body: Before your next tricky topic, ask your partner when would be a good time to talk.

lessons.title: Hear the Feeling
lessons.summary: Listen for what matters beneath the words.

steps.title: Facts on top, feelings underneath
steps.body: When your partner vents about their day, the details matter less than how it left them feeling. That’s the part they most want you to catch.

steps.prompt: Your partner walks in and says, “Today was a nightmare.” What’s the best first response?

options.text: “That sounds exhausting. Want to tell me about it?”
options.why: It names the feeling and invites them in, without steering the conversation anywhere.

options.text: “Mine was worse, honestly.”
options.why: Comparing days turns their moment into a contest, and they’re likely to stop sharing.

options.text: “Well, at least it’s over now.”
options.why: Meant kindly, but it hurries past the feeling before they’ve had a chance to say it.

steps.title: Name it, then wait
steps.body: Offer a feeling word: “frustrating”, “lonely”, “a lot”. If you guess wrong they’ll correct you, and that still helps them feel heard.

steps.prompt: Reflect the feeling back.
steps.before: It sounds like today was really
steps.why: A guess at their feeling shows you’re tuned in; the other two judge it or shrink it.

steps.prompt: When your partner is upset, what’s your first instinct?
steps.reply: Every one of those comes from care. Leading with listening just helps the rest land better.

steps.title: A cancelled birthday

lines.text: My sister just cancelled my birthday dinner. Again.

steps.prompt: What do you send back?

options.text: Don’t let it get to you, she’s always been like that.
options.why: It brushes the hurt aside, so they’re left feeling it alone.

options.text: Oh love, that really stings, especially three years in a row. I’m sorry. 💛
options.reaction: It really does. Thank you for getting it.
options.why: You named the feeling and why it makes sense, which is what helps someone feel heard.

options.text: Want me to book somewhere for just us two instead?
options.reaction: Maybe… I’m still just annoyed though.
options.why: A kind idea, but jumping to fix it skips the part where they feel understood.

steps.body: Tonight, when your partner tells you about their day, name the feeling you hear before offering anything else.

lessons.title: Reflect It Back
lessons.summary: Say back what you heard before you respond.

steps.title: Show them you got it
steps.body: Reflecting means saying back the heart of what they said, in your own words: “So you felt invisible in that meeting.” It proves you heard them, and gives them a chance to correct you.

steps.prompt: Your partner says, “My sister keeps making plans for Mum’s birthday without asking me.” Which reply reflects it best?

options.text: “Just plan your own thing, then.”
options.why: That’s advice. They may not feel heard yet.

options.text: “Sounds like you feel left out of decisions about your own mum.”
options.why: It names the feeling underneath, which shows real understanding.

options.text: “Your sister has always been bossy.”
options.why: It takes a side but skips how they actually feel.

steps.prompt: A reflecting starter.
steps.why: “What I’m hearing” keeps the focus on their words, not your opinion.

steps.prompt: When your partner shares a problem, your first instinct is to…
steps.reply: Every instinct is caring. Reflecting first just makes the rest land better.

steps.prompt: Match each statement with a reflection.
steps.why: A good reflection names the feeling behind the words, so your partner feels understood rather than just answered.

steps.body: Next time your partner vents, reflect back what you heard before you offer any view.

lessons.title: Ask, Then Ask Again
lessons.summary: A second question shows you want the whole story.

steps.title: The second question goes deeper
steps.body: The first question often gets the headline. A gentle follow-up like “And how did that feel?” or “What part bothered you most?” is where the real story is.

steps.prompt: Your partner says their performance review went “fine, I guess”. What’s the best follow-up?

options.text: “Great!” and change the subject.
options.why: “I guess” was a hint, and moving on misses it.

options.text: “Only fine? You should have prepared more.”
options.why: Judging now shuts the door they half opened.

options.text: “Fine, I guess? What part are you unsure about?”
options.why: You noticed their hesitation and gently invited more.

steps.prompt: Invite the rest.
steps.why: Asking about the hardest part lets them share what really matters.

steps.prompt: How often do you ask a second question?
steps.reply: Just one more gentle question each day can make your partner feel much more known.

steps.prompt: Going deeper. Put these in order.
steps.why: Facts, then feelings, then needs. By the time you offer help, you know what kind of help they want.

steps.body: Today, ask your partner one follow-up question after their first answer.

lessons.title: Tiny Moments Matter
lessons.summary: Notice everyday invitations to connect.

steps.title: Small bids, big signals
steps.body: “Look at that!” “Guess what happened?” These little invitations are called bids. How you answer them, day after day, shapes how close you feel.

steps.title: Three ways to answer
steps.body: You can turn towards a bid (respond), turn away (miss it) or turn against it (snap). Turning towards often takes just a few seconds.

steps.prompt: On a walk, your partner points out a ridiculous-looking bird. Which response turns towards the bid?

options.text: Keep scrolling and say, “Mm-hm.”
options.why: One missed bid feels tiny, but lots of them add up to feeling alone together.

options.text: “Take a photo, I’ll look later.”
options.why: It postpones the moment, and by later the shared fun of it has gone.

options.text: Stop, look and laugh: “It looks so grumpy!”
options.why: A few seconds of shared attention tells them their small moments matter to you.

steps.prompt: Which bids from your partner are easiest for you to miss?
steps.reply: Spotting your blind spot makes those bids much easier to catch this week.

steps.prompt: Match each bid with a way to turn towards it.

pairs.a: A sigh while reading the news
A funny meme sent at lunch
pairs.b: A reply that shows you laughed

steps.why: Bids are small reaches for attention. Turning towards them, even briefly, is what builds closeness over time.

steps.body: Notice the small bids your partner makes today, and turn towards at least three of them.

lessons.title: Daily Check-Ins
lessons.summary: Ten minutes a day keeps you on the same page.

steps.title: A small daily ritual
steps.body: Couples who spend even ten minutes a day talking about their lives, not logistics, stay closer. It’s not about the length, it’s about it happening most days.

steps.prompt: You both get home tired every evening. What’s the most realistic way to stay connected?

options.text: Ten minutes over tea, phones away, swapping highs and lows.
options.why: Short, regular and easy to keep up, even on busy days.

options.text: Save it all for a long talk at the weekend.
options.why: Weekends fill up, and a week’s worth of small news gets lost.

options.text: Text each other updates through the day instead.
options.why: Handy, but it can’t replace looking up and talking.

steps.prompt: Keep it about life, not lists.
steps.why: Asking for a good moment keeps the check-in warm, not a to-do list.

steps.prompt: When could a daily check-in fit into your routine?
steps.reply: Tying it to something you already do makes it far easier to keep.

steps.prompt: Real check-in, or just logistics?
steps.why: Logistics run the house. Check-ins keep you knowing each other, and both need their own time.

steps.body: Tonight, spend ten phone-free minutes asking about your partner’s day, not your plans.

lessons.title: Affection Out Loud
lessons.summary: Say the warm things you usually only think.

steps.title: Fondness needs saying
steps.body: We often notice what our partner does wrong and stay silent about what they do right. Saying the warm things out loud builds a cushion that helps you through harder days.

steps.prompt: Your partner made you a packed lunch on a stressful day. What’s the best response?

options.text: Say nothing. They know you appreciate it.
options.why: They may not. Unspoken thanks can start to feel like being taken for granted.

options.text: “That was so thoughtful. It made my rough morning better. Thank you.”
options.why: Specific thanks shows you noticed and that it mattered.

options.text: “Thanks, but I’d already planned to buy lunch.”
options.why: The “but” turns kindness into a correction.

steps.prompt: Name what you love.
steps.why: Specific appreciation lands deeper than a general “you’re great”.

steps.prompt: Write one thing you appreciate about your partner that you haven’t said lately.
steps.placeholder: e.g. how patient you were with my mum

steps.prompt: Match each moment with a warm thing to say.
steps.why: Small, specific compliments, said often, keep fondness alive through busy and stressful seasons.

steps.body: Say one specific, warm thing to your partner today that you’d normally only think.

lessons.title: Love in Their Language
lessons.summary: Show love in the way they most feel it.

steps.title: People feel loved differently
steps.body: Some feel loved through words, others through help, touch, time together or small gifts. If you show love only in your way, your partner may miss it.

steps.prompt: Your partner lights up when you help with chores, but you mostly show love with compliments. What helps most?

options.text: Keep complimenting. It’s how you show love.
options.why: Kind, but it may not land the way you hope.

options.text: Ask them what makes them feel most cared for.
options.why: A good start, but you’ve already spotted a clear clue.

options.text: Add more practical help, like doing the school run.
options.why: You’re speaking their language, so your love is easier for them to feel.

steps.prompt: Find out directly.
steps.why: Asking is the simplest way to stop guessing what matters to them.

steps.prompt: How do you most feel loved?
steps.reply: Sharing this with your partner helps them love you in a way you’ll notice.

steps.prompt: Words or actions?

cards.text: Taking the early shift with the baby

steps.why: Both are love. Noticing which your partner responds to helps your care land where it counts.

steps.body: Ask your partner what makes them feel most loved, and do one thing in that way this week.

lessons.title: Say What You Need
lessons.summary: Make room for closeness and personal space.

steps.title: Needing space isn’t rejection
steps.body: Wanting quiet after a long day doesn’t mean you love your partner any less. Saying so clearly protects both your energy and your closeness.

steps.prompt: You’re drained and need quiet, but your partner wants to talk the moment you get home. What helps most?

options.text: Push through the chat while getting more irritable.
options.why: They’ll feel the irritation without knowing why, and the chat goes worse for you both.

options.text: Head to another room without a word.
options.why: Silence leaves them guessing, and many people read it as you being upset with them.

options.text: “I want to hear it. Can I have 20 minutes to recharge first?”
options.why: It shows you care, names your need and gives a clear time, so it doesn’t feel like a brush-off.

steps.title: Add a bridge back
steps.body: The kindest boundaries come with a plan to reconnect: “I need an hour to myself, then let’s cook together.” Space feels safer when it has an end.

steps.prompt: Add the bridge back.
steps.why: It pairs your need with a promise to return, so your partner feels included, not shut out.

steps.prompt: What do you need more of at home, and how could you ask for it?
Asking for quiet time. Put these in order.
steps.why: Spotting it early lets you ask calmly; a time limit and a plan to reconnect show it’s about rest, not distance.

steps.body: Name one need to your partner today, and say when you’ll reconnect afterwards.

lessons.title: Ask Without Hinting
lessons.summary: Clear asks beat hoping they’ll guess.

steps.title: Hints are easy to miss
steps.body: “It would be nice if someone emptied the dishwasher” feels like asking, but it often gets missed, then resented. A clear, kind ask is more likely to get you what you need.

steps.prompt: You’d love more help planning date nights, which you’ve always organised. What’s the clearest way to ask?

options.text: “Could you plan our next date night? I’d love to be surprised.”
options.why: Specific, warm and easy to say yes to.

options.text: “Must be nice never having to plan anything.”
options.why: Sarcasm hides the request and adds a sting.

options.text: Stop planning and see if they notice.
options.why: A silent test often ends with both of you disappointed.

steps.prompt: Make the ask clear.
steps.after: to take the bins out on Mondays?
steps.why: “Would you be willing” is a real question, so they can say yes freely.

steps.prompt: What do you tend to hint at instead of asking for?
steps.reply: Turning that hint into a kind, clear ask is a quick win for you both.

steps.prompt: Match each hint with a clear ask.

pairs.b: “Could I have an hour to rest?”

steps.why: Hints rely on mind-reading. Clear asks give your partner a fair chance to help.

steps.body: Turn one hint you often drop into a clear, kind request this week.

lessons.title: Space Without Distance
lessons.summary: Time apart can bring you closer.

steps.title: Space is healthy
steps.body: Wanting time for your own friends and hobbies isn’t a sign of trouble. Explained kindly, it helps you come back with more energy, and more to share.

steps.prompt: Your partner wants a weekend away with their friends. You feel a bit left out. What’s healthiest?

options.text: Agree, then sulk until they cancel.
options.why: Sulking makes them choose between you and their friends.

options.text: “Have a great time! Could we plan something together the weekend after?”
options.why: You support their space and ask for connection, without guilt.

options.text: Say you’re fine, then book plans for that exact weekend.
options.why: Tit-for-tat creates distance rather than balance.

steps.prompt: Explain your need kindly.
steps.before: I need some time on my own, and it’s not about
steps.why: Saying it isn’t about them stops alone time feeling like rejection.

steps.prompt: How do you feel when your partner wants time apart?
steps.reply: Any of these is normal. Talking about it openly helps you find a rhythm you both like.

steps.title: A solo afternoon

lines.text: Would you mind if I went to the climbing wall on my own Saturday?
I just need a few hours to switch off.

steps.prompt: Reply:

options.text: Of course! Enjoy it. Fancy a takeaway together after?
options.why: You give space freely and add a moment to reconnect.

options.text: I guess I’ll just sit here alone then.
options.why: Guilt makes their need feel wrong and builds resentment.

options.text: Why do you need a break from me?
options.why: Taking it personally turns a simple ask into a worry.

steps.body: Encourage your partner to do one thing just for themselves this week, and plan a reconnect after.

lessons.title: Build Everyday Trust
lessons.summary: Let reliability grow through small promises.

steps.title: Trust grows in small deposits
steps.body: Trust comes less from grand gestures and more from ordinary reliability: being where you said, doing what you said and owning it when you don’t.

steps.prompt: You promised to book the dentist for you both, then forgot. Your partner asks about it. What builds trust?

options.text: “It’s not a big deal, it can wait.”
options.why: It may feel small to you, but brushing it off tells them their reminders don’t count.

options.text: “I forgot, I’m sorry. I’ll book it on my lunch break today.”
options.why: Owning it and naming a specific fix shows you can be relied on, even when you slip.

options.text: “The booking site wasn’t working.”
options.why: Small excuses feel harmless, but if they’re found out, trust takes a much bigger hit.

steps.prompt: Make a promise you can keep.
steps.why: Specific and realistic beats vague or over-ambitious, and it’s easy to see you did it.

steps.title: Trust is never about fear
steps.body: Healthy relationships never involve fear, control or harm. If something in yours feels unsafe, talking to someone you trust or a local support line can help.

steps.prompt: Which kind of promise do you find hardest to keep?
steps.reply: That’s a good place to start: one smaller, clearer promise in that area builds trust fastest.

steps.prompt: Builds trust or chips away at it?

cards.text: Doing what you said, even small things
“I’ll do it later” that never happens
Telling them early when plans change
Hiding a small purchase to avoid a talk
Owning it when you get it wrong

steps.why: Trust grows from many small moments of keeping your word and being honest, especially when it’s awkward.

steps.body: Keep one small promise today exactly as you said, or give an honest update before it’s due.

lessons.title: Small Truths Matter
lessons.summary: Honesty about little things protects the big ones.

steps.title: Little fibs add up
steps.body: “I only spent a bit” or “I’m nearly home” when you haven’t left feel harmless. But when small things don’t match, partners start to wonder what else doesn’t.

steps.prompt: You bought expensive trainers you know your partner will think are pricey. They ask how much they were. What builds trust?

options.text: Knock a bit off the price.
options.why: If it comes out, the fib hurts more than the trainers ever would.

options.text: Change the subject.
options.why: Dodging makes them wonder why you won’t say.

options.text: “More than I usually spend, honestly. They were a treat.”
options.why: Being straight, even when it’s awkward, shows your word can be relied on.

steps.prompt: Honest, even when awkward.
steps.before: I’d rather tell you now than have you
steps.why: Getting ahead of an awkward truth shows respect and keeps trust steady.

steps.prompt: Which small fib is most tempting for you?
steps.reply: Noticing your temptation is the first step to choosing honesty instead.

steps.prompt: Builds trust, or quietly erodes it?

cards.text: “I’m on my way” before you’ve left
Hiding a shopping bag in the car
Admitting you forgot to do something

steps.why: Honest small moments make your partner feel safe believing you when it really counts.

steps.body: Today, choose the honest version of one small thing you’d usually smooth over.

lessons.title: Keep Them in the Loop
lessons.summary: A quick update saves a lot of worry.

steps.title: Updates are a kind of care
steps.body: A two-second text saying you’ll be late, or that plans changed, stops your partner worrying or feeling forgotten. Being predictable is part of being trustworthy.

steps.prompt: You’re invited for drinks after work and will be home two hours later than usual. What’s best?

options.text: Go, and explain when you get home.
options.why: They might worry, or have planned dinner for you.

options.text: Text: “Colleagues are going for a drink. Okay if I’m home around 9?”
options.why: A quick heads-up keeps them included and avoids surprise.

options.text: Don’t go, so you don’t have to explain.
options.why: You don’t need to miss out. A message is all it takes.

steps.prompt: A quick heads-up.
steps.after: , I’ll be back a bit later tonight.
steps.why: Simple updates show you’re thinking of them, even when apart.

steps.prompt: How do you usually let your partner know about changes?
steps.reply: Whatever your style, making updates a habit is a quiet way to build trust.

steps.prompt: When plans change. Put these in order.
steps.why: A fast, clear update, plus checking how it lands for them, makes changes feel shared rather than sprung.

steps.body: Send your partner a quick heads-up the next time your plans change, however small.

lessons.title: Pause the Argument
lessons.summary: Cool down without abandoning the conversation.

steps.title: When the heat takes over
steps.body: In a heated argument your heart races and listening gets harder. Pushing on rarely helps; a short, agreed pause usually does.

steps.prompt: You’re arguing about money and your voices are rising. What’s the most helpful move?

options.text: “I’m getting worked up. Can we take 20 minutes and come back?”
options.why: It owns your state, sets a time and promises to return, so it’s a pause rather than an escape.

options.text: Walk out and say you’re done talking about it.
options.why: Leaving with no return time can feel like abandonment, and the issue stays unsolved.

options.text: Keep arguing until one of you gives in.
options.why: Someone may give in, but nobody feels understood, and the same fight tends to come back.

steps.title: Use the break well
steps.body: Do something calming, like a walk or some music, rather than replaying the argument in your head. Then come back when you said you would.

steps.prompt: Make the pause feel safe.
words: come back to it at eight
steps.answer: come back to it at eight
steps.why: A set time reassures your partner the conversation matters and isn’t being dodged.

steps.prompt: When an argument heats up, what do you tend to do?
steps.reply: Each of those is a way of coping. An agreed pause gives you something better to reach for.

steps.prompt: Taking a time-out in a fight. Put these in order.
steps.why: A pause only helps if you ask for it kindly and return; calming your body first lets you actually hear each other.

steps.body: While you’re both calm, agree a pause signal with your partner and how long a break should last.

lessons.title: Spot the Flood
lessons.summary: Notice when your body has taken over the argument.

steps.title: Flooding stops good listening
steps.body: When your heart races, your jaw tightens and you can’t think straight, you’re “flooded”. In that state nobody listens well. Spotting it early is the key to stopping a fight spiralling.

steps.prompt: Mid-argument, you notice your heart pounding and you can only think of comebacks. What’s happening?

options.text: You’re winning the argument.
options.why: It may feel that way, but your body is in fight mode, not problem-solving mode.

options.text: You’re flooded, and need a short break to calm down.
options.why: Naming it lets you pause before saying something you’ll regret.

options.text: Your partner is being unreasonable.
options.why: They might be, but your flooded brain can’t judge that fairly right now.

steps.prompt: Name it out loud.
steps.after: . Can we take a short break?
steps.why: Naming your state, not their fault, makes a pause feel safe rather than like walking out.

steps.prompt: What’s your first sign of getting flooded?
steps.reply: Knowing your early warning sign means you can pause before things escalate.

steps.prompt: Match each sign with what it means.

pairs.b: Your body is in fight mode

steps.why: These signs mean your thinking brain is offline. A short break, then a return, works far better than pushing on.

steps.body: Notice your own flooding sign in the next tense moment, and name it before you react.

lessons.title: One Topic at a Time
lessons.summary: Don’t throw every old issue into one fight.

steps.title: Kitchen-sinking
steps.body: An argument about the dishes can quickly pull in last Christmas, their mother and money. Piling in old issues makes every problem impossible to solve. One topic at a time keeps it fixable.

steps.prompt: You’re arguing about who forgot to book the car service, and you want to mention how they forgot your anniversary. What’s best?

options.text: Bring it up. It proves the pattern.
options.why: It widens the fight and makes them defend everything at once.

options.text: Stick to the car, and raise the anniversary another time if it still matters.
options.why: Keeping to one topic lets you actually solve it.

options.text: List every time they’ve forgotten something.
options.why: A list of failures feels like an attack, not a conversation.

steps.prompt: Bring it back.
steps.why: Gently steering back to one issue keeps the talk solvable.

steps.prompt: Which old issue tends to sneak into your arguments?
steps.reply: If it keeps coming up, it may deserve its own calm conversation.

steps.prompt: On topic, or kitchen-sinking?

cards.text: “About the service, can we set a reminder?”
“This is just like what your dad does.”
“Let’s sort this, then talk about the other thing later.”

steps.why: Staying on one topic keeps arguments short and solvable. Old issues deserve their own, calmer time.

steps.body: In your next disagreement, gently say “one thing at a time” if other issues creep in.

lessons.title: Find the Dream Inside
lessons.summary: Some fights are about deeper hopes, not surface details.

steps.title: Stuck fights hide a dream
steps.body: Couples often have the same argument for years: money, where to live, how tidy to be. Underneath is usually a deeper hope, like security or freedom. Understanding that hope can unstick it.

steps.prompt: You keep arguing because your partner wants to save every spare penny, and you want to travel. What helps most?

options.text: “What does saving mean to you? What would it protect?”
options.why: Curiosity about the hope underneath helps you find a plan that honours both of you.

options.text: Prove with numbers that you can afford a trip.
options.why: Logic rarely shifts a fight that’s really about feelings.

options.text: Agree to stop talking about it.
options.why: Avoiding it keeps the frustration simmering on both sides.

steps.prompt: Ask about the deeper hope.
steps.why: That one question moves you from positions to the hopes behind them.

steps.prompt: Think of an argument you keep having. What might the deeper hope be, for each of you?
steps.placeholder: e.g. They want security, I want adventure

steps.prompt: Match each stance with a possible hope underneath.
steps.why: Once you see the hope behind a stance, you can look for ways to honour both, rather than one person winning.

steps.body: Ask your partner about the deeper hope behind one thing you often disagree on, and just listen.

lessons.title: Repair After a Slip
lessons.summary: An apology can open a door to repair.

steps.title: Everyone snaps sometimes
steps.body: Strong couples aren’t the ones who never hurt each other. They’re the ones who notice it and repair it, quickly and sincerely.

steps.prompt: You snapped at your partner after a stressful commute. A little later, what repairs it best?

options.text: “Sorry, but you were winding me up.”
options.why: The “but” cancels the apology and hands the blame straight back to them.

options.text: Be extra nice all evening and never mention it.
options.why: Kindness helps, but without words the hurt can linger, unspoken, between you.

options.text: “I was sharp with you earlier. I’m sorry, you didn’t deserve that.”
options.why: It names exactly what you did and takes responsibility, which makes it easy to accept.

steps.title: What makes an apology land
steps.body: Name what you did, own the impact and skip the excuses. You can add what you’ll try next time. Short and specific beats long and dramatic.

steps.prompt: Own the impact.
steps.after: I’ll try to pause next time.
steps.why: It owns the effect on them. Excuses, even true ones, make an apology feel half-hearted.

steps.prompt: What makes apologising hardest for you?
steps.reply: Completely human. A short, specific apology is enough, and it gets easier every time.

steps.title: The night out

lines.text: Can I say something? You were on your phone most of my friend’s dinner.
I felt a bit on my own tonight.

steps.prompt: How do you reply?

options.text: I was only checking work stuff for a minute.
options.reaction: It was more than a minute 😕
options.why: Defending the detail misses how they felt, so the hurt stays open.

options.text: Well, your friends aren’t easy to talk to.
options.why: Turning it back on them makes it a new argument instead of a repair.

options.text: You’re right, I was distracted. I’m sorry you felt alone. Can we try again next time?
options.reaction: Thanks for hearing me. Yes, let’s 💛
options.why: You owned it, named their feeling and offered to do better, which is what makes a repair land.

steps.body: Think of a recent sharp moment and offer your partner a short, specific apology, with no “but”.

lessons.title: Accept Their Repair
lessons.summary: When they reach out mid-fight, reach back.

steps.title: Repair attempts need catching
steps.body: In a tense moment, your partner might make a joke, touch your arm or say “okay, I hear you.” These are repair attempts. Accepting them, even a little, turns the fight around.

steps.prompt: Mid-argument, your partner says, “Can we start again? I don’t want to fight.” You’re still annoyed. What do you do?

options.text: “No, you need to hear this.”
options.why: Rejecting the repair keeps you both stuck in the fight.

options.text: Ignore it and carry on making your point.
options.why: It may feel like they don’t care, when they’re trying to.

options.text: “Okay. I’m still a bit annoyed, but yes, let’s start again.”
options.why: You can be honest about your feelings and still accept their olive branch.

steps.prompt: Accept the olive branch.
steps.why: Meeting their repair halfway is often all it takes to calm things down.

steps.prompt: How does your partner usually try to repair?
steps.reply: Learning their style helps you spot the olive branch when it comes.

steps.title: A silly face

lines.text: Okay, I hear you about the washing. I’m sorry.

steps.prompt: You were still mid-rant. Reply:

options.text: Don’t try to make me laugh.
options.why: Turning down a repair can make your partner stop trying next time.

options.text: Ha, okay. Truce 🏳️ Thank you for saying that.
options.why: Accepting the repair turns the moment around and protects you both.

options.text: You always do this to get out of things.
options.why: Treating a repair as a trick reopens the fight.

steps.body: Next time your partner tries to ease a tense moment, meet them halfway.

lessons.title: After the Storm
lessons.summary: Talk about the fight once you’re both calm.

steps.title: Learn from each argument
steps.body: Once you’ve both calmed down, a short, kind chat about what happened stops the same fight repeating. Not to win, but to understand what each of you was feeling.

steps.prompt: The day after a big argument, things feel okay again. What’s most helpful?

options.text: Never mention it again. It’s over.
options.why: Unspoken feelings often come back in the next fight.

options.text: “Can we talk about yesterday? I want to understand what upset you.”
options.why: A calm look back helps you both learn and feel heard.

options.text: Remind them what they said that hurt you.
options.why: Starting with blame tends to restart the argument.

steps.prompt: Own your part.
steps.after: in it was raising my voice.
steps.why: Naming your own part first makes it easier for your partner to name theirs.

steps.prompt: After a fight, you usually…
steps.reply: A short, calm debrief, even ten minutes, can save you from the same fight next month.

steps.prompt: A calm debrief. Put these in order.
items: Agree one thing to try next time
steps.why: Feelings first, then ownership, then a small plan. That way the talk heals rather than re-argues.

steps.body: After your next disagreement, suggest a calm ten-minute debrief once you’ve both cooled down.

lessons.title: Share the Load
lessons.summary: Talk fairly about invisible household work.

steps.title: The work nobody sees
steps.body: Remembering birthdays, planning meals, noticing the milk’s running low: this “mental load” is real work, and carrying it alone breeds resentment.

steps.title: Own it, don’t just help
steps.body: Helping when asked still leaves one person managing everything. Owning a task means you notice it, plan it and finish it, without reminders.

steps.prompt: Your partner seems stressed juggling meals, bills and appointments. What helps most?

options.text: Ask which jobs feel heaviest and take full ownership of one or two.
options.why: Owning a task from start to finish lifts the planning burden, not just the doing.

options.text: Ask them to give you a list of what to do.
options.why: Kind, but they still have to notice, plan and hand out jobs, which is the tiring part.

options.text: Point out that you both work hard, so it’s even.
options.why: It skips past how they actually feel, and they may stop raising it altogether.

steps.prompt: Offer real ownership.
steps.why: A clearly owned job takes the remembering off their plate, not just the errand.

steps.prompt: Which household job could you fully own, from start to finish?
Match each vague ask with a clear one.

pairs.b: “Could you do the bins on Tuesdays?”
“Could you do two school runs a week?”

steps.why: Vague asks sound like criticism and are hard to act on; clear ones say exactly what would help.

steps.body: Pick one recurring job and own it this week, from noticing it’s needed to getting it done, without a reminder.

lessons.title: Notice the Invisible Work
lessons.summary: Planning and remembering are work too.

steps.title: The mental load
steps.body: Remembering birthdays, booking appointments, noticing the milk is low. This invisible planning is real work, and it often falls on one person without anyone noticing.

steps.prompt: Your partner seems frazzled, though you both do equal chores. What might be going on?

options.text: They’re probably just tired from work.
options.why: Maybe, but you might be missing a load you can’t see.

options.text: They may be carrying the planning and remembering, on top of chores.
options.why: Invisible tasks are draining, and noticing them is the first step to sharing them.

options.text: Nothing. The chores are split evenly.
options.why: Doing tasks isn’t the same as keeping track of all of them.

steps.prompt: Take full ownership.
steps.why: Owning a task from start to finish takes the mental load, not just the doing.

steps.prompt: Who keeps track of most of the planning in your home?
steps.reply: Talking openly about the invisible work is often a relief for both of you.

steps.prompt: Visible chore, or invisible work?

cards.text: Noticing the kids need new shoes
Planning what’s for dinner all week

steps.why: Invisible work takes time and headspace. Seeing it is what makes a fair split possible.

steps.body: Take full ownership of one piece of invisible planning this week, from remembering to finishing.

lessons.title: Plan the Week Together
lessons.summary: A short weekly chat stops a lot of friction.

steps.title: A weekly planning chat
steps.body: Fifteen minutes on a Sunday to look at the week ahead, who’s doing what, when you’ll see each other, means fewer surprises and fewer “I thought you were doing it” moments.

steps.prompt: You keep double-booking evenings and clashing over who does what. What would help most?

options.text: A short Sunday chat to plan the week together.
options.why: A regular check-in means you share the load and avoid surprises.

options.text: Each keep your own diary and hope it works out.
options.why: That’s how double-bookings happen.

options.text: One person decides and tells the other.
options.why: Quicker, but the planner ends up carrying it all.

steps.prompt: Make it shared.
steps.before: Let’s put both our plans in a
steps.why: One shared calendar means you both see the whole week at a glance.

steps.prompt: What would you most like to plan together each week?
steps.reply: Starting with just one of these makes the habit easy to begin.

steps.title: Sunday evening

lines.text: Wait, you’re out Wednesday too? I booked the plumber for then 😩

steps.prompt: What do you suggest?

options.text: Ugh, sorry. Shall we do a quick plan every Sunday so this stops happening?
options.reaction: Yes please. Ten minutes, with tea ☕
options.why: You own the slip and suggest a simple fix that helps you both.

options.text: Well, you should have checked with me.
options.why: Blame turns a planning mix-up into an argument.

options.text: I’ll just cancel my plans then.
options.why: Giving in fixes today but not the pattern.

steps.body: Suggest a ten-minute weekly planning chat with your partner, and try it this Sunday.

lessons.title: Stay Curious
lessons.summary: Replace assumptions with honest questions.

steps.title: The stories we tell ourselves
steps.body: When a partner seems distant, our minds rush to explain it, often with the worst version. Curiosity checks the story before you believe it.

steps.prompt: Your partner has been quieter than usual all week. What’s the most trusting next step?

options.text: Decide they’re annoyed with you and go quiet too.
options.why: Acting on a guess can create the very distance you were worried about.

options.text: “You’ve seemed quiet lately. How are you doing?”
options.why: It shares what you’ve noticed without blame and lets them tell you what’s really going on.

options.text: Look through their phone to find out why.
options.why: Checking in secret damages trust far more than one quiet week ever could.

steps.title: Notice, ask, then listen
steps.body: Share what you’ve seen, ask an open question, then really listen. If they’re not ready to talk, let them know you’re around when they are.

steps.prompt: Ask, don’t accuse.
steps.why: Describing what you see invites an answer; the others assume a reason and spark a defence.

steps.prompt: When your partner seems off, what does your mind jump to first?
steps.reply: Whatever your mind jumps to, it’s only a guess until you ask them.

steps.title: Something on their mind

lines.text: Nothing bad! Just something that’s been on my mind.

steps.prompt: What do you send?

options.text: Of course. Thanks for telling me. I’ll make tea and we can talk after dinner. ☕
options.why: You stay calm, thank them and make space, which makes it easy for them to open up.

options.text: That sounds ominous… what did I do?
options.reaction: Nothing! Honestly, it’s not about you.
options.why: Jumping to the worst makes it about you and can make them wary of raising things.

options.text: Can’t you just tell me now?
options.reaction: I’d rather talk properly, in person.
options.why: Pushing for it now ignores the way they asked to have the talk.

steps.body: Check in about one change you’ve noticed in your partner, describing what you saw rather than what you assumed.

lessons.title: Update Your Map
lessons.summary: Keep learning who your partner is now.

steps.title: People keep changing
steps.body: The person you met has new worries, hopes and favourite things now. Couples who keep asking about each other’s inner world stay close through all the changes.

steps.prompt: You realise you don’t know what your partner is most worried about at the moment. What’s best?

options.text: Assume it’s the same as last year.
options.why: Life moves on, and an old answer may not fit any more.

options.text: Wait for them to bring it up.
options.why: Some worries stay quiet unless someone asks.

options.text: “What’s weighing on you most these days?”
options.why: A simple, open question keeps your knowledge of them up to date.

steps.prompt: Keep asking.
steps.why: Asking about hopes, not just worries, shows you care about their whole life.

steps.prompt: How well do you know your partner’s current hopes and worries?
steps.reply: Whatever your answer, a few curious questions this week will help.

steps.prompt: Match each area with a question to ask.

pairs.b: “What’s the best part of it now?”
“Who have you felt close to lately?”

steps.why: Questions across different parts of life help you see your partner as they are now, not as they were.

steps.body: Ask your partner one question this week you’ve never asked before.

lessons.title: Big Questions
lessons.summary: Go beyond the everyday sometimes.

steps.title: Deeper talks bring you closer
steps.body: Most couple talk is logistics. Every so often, a bigger question, like “What do you want our life to feel like in five years?”, can bring a fresh sense of closeness.

steps.prompt: You’re on a quiet walk together. Which question is most likely to spark a deeper talk?

options.text: “Did you remember to book the MOT?”
options.why: Useful, but it keeps you in logistics mode.

options.text: “What’s something you’ve changed your mind about this year?”
options.why: Open and personal, it invites a real conversation.

options.text: “Nice weather, isn’t it?”
options.why: Pleasant, but it’s hard to go deeper from there.

steps.prompt: A big question.
steps.before: What would make next year feel
steps.why: Questions about meaning invite your partner to share what truly matters to them.

steps.prompt: When do you and your partner have your best talks?
steps.reply: Saving a big question for those moments makes deeper talks feel natural.

steps.prompt: Everyday question, or a big one?

cards.text: “What do you hope our kids remember?”

steps.why: Everyday questions run your life together; big ones remind you why you share it.

steps.body: On your next quiet moment together, ask your partner one big question and really listen.

lessons.title: Support Their Dreams
lessons.summary: Be your partner’s biggest supporter.

steps.title: Dreams need a cheerleader
steps.body: When a partner shares a dream, like a new career or a big trip, the response matters. Interest and support make them feel safe to dream; doubt makes them hide their hopes.

steps.prompt: Your partner says they’re thinking of training to be a nurse. It would mean less money for a while. What’s the best first response?

options.text: “That’s exciting! What’s drawing you to it?”
options.why: You show interest first, and can talk through the practical side together later.

options.text: “We can’t afford that.”
options.why: Leading with doubt can make them shelve the dream without exploring it.

options.text: “Are you sure? It’s really hard work.”
options.why: Fair point, but too soon. It can sound like you don’t believe in them.

steps.prompt: Show you believe in them.
steps.why: Hearing you believe in them gives them courage to take the first step.

steps.prompt: What’s one dream your partner has mentioned? How could you support it?
steps.placeholder: e.g. help them find a pottery class

steps.prompt: Supporting a dream. Put these in order.
items: Ask what it means to them
steps.why: Interest and understanding come first, so planning feels like teamwork rather than a reality check.

steps.body: Ask your partner about a dream they have, and offer to help with one small first step.

lessons.title: Choose Us Again
lessons.summary: Create a small ritual that lasts.

steps.title: Love needs regular tending
steps.body: Busy weeks can quietly turn partners into flatmates. Closeness rarely fixes itself; it grows back through small moments you choose on purpose.

steps.prompt: Work and life have left you both feeling disconnected. What’s the best first step?

options.text: Wait for your next holiday to reconnect.
options.why: Holidays help, but months of distance before then can make the gap feel wider.

options.text: Suggest ten phone-free minutes together every evening.
options.why: Small, regular rituals are easier to keep than big plans, and they add up quickly.

options.text: Assume real love shouldn’t take any effort.
options.why: Every lasting relationship takes effort; needing it is a sign of care, not of trouble.

steps.title: Make it a ritual
steps.body: Morning coffee together, a Sunday walk, a goodnight check-in. The best rituals are short, regular and something you both look forward to.

steps.prompt: When do you feel most connected to your partner?
steps.reply: That’s your starting point. Build a small ritual around it and protect it in your week.

steps.prompt: What small ritual could you two start this week?
Brings you closer or lets you drift?

cards.text: A phone-free dinner once a week
Talking only about chores and bills
Asking, “What’s been on your mind lately?”
A six-second hug when you get home

steps.why: Closeness comes back through small, regular rituals of attention, not just big gestures or holidays.

steps.body: Suggest one small weekly ritual to your partner and put the first one in both your diaries.

lessons.title: Date Night, Reimagined
lessons.summary: Fresh experiences keep the spark alive.

steps.title: Novelty brings you closer
steps.body: Doing something new together, even something small, gives you the same buzz you felt early on. A new walk, a cooking class or a game night can beat the usual restaurant.

steps.prompt: Your date nights have become the same pizza and film every Friday. What would refresh things most?

options.text: Keep the routine. It’s comfortable.
options.why: Comfort is lovely, but some newness helps the spark stay alive.

options.text: Take turns planning something neither of you has tried before.
options.why: Shared newness and taking turns keep it fresh and fair.

options.text: Skip date night. You see each other every day.
options.why: Seeing each other isn’t the same as focused time together.

steps.prompt: Try something fresh.
steps.why: New experiences create new memories, and remind you why you enjoy each other.

steps.prompt: What new thing would you love to try together?
steps.reply: Suggest it this week, and let your partner pick the next one.

steps.prompt: Match each usual date with a fresh twist.
steps.why: Small twists on familiar dates bring the excitement of something new, without a big budget.

steps.body: Plan one date with your partner this month that’s new to both of you.

lessons.title: Celebrate Your Story
lessons.summary: Remember how far you’ve come together.

steps.title: Your shared story matters
steps.body: Couples who remember their good times fondly, the funny first date, the hard year you got through, feel more like a team. Retelling your story strengthens it.

steps.prompt: Your anniversary is coming up, but money is tight. What’s most meaningful?

options.text: Skip it this year.
options.why: Marking it doesn’t have to cost much, and skipping it can feel sad.

options.text: An expensive meal on a credit card.
options.why: Lovely in the moment, but the stress afterwards may outweigh it.

options.text: Revisit your first date spot and share favourite memories.
options.why: It honours your story without stretching your budget.

steps.prompt: Remember together.
steps.before: Do you remember the time we
steps.why: Shared happy memories remind you both of the team you’ve built.

steps.prompt: What’s a favourite memory of you and your partner?
steps.placeholder: e.g. dancing in the kitchen during the power cut

steps.title: A memory

lines.text: Just found the photo from our first holiday 😂

steps.prompt: Reply:

options.text: Ha, nice.
options.why: A flat reply misses the chance to enjoy the memory together.

options.text: Delete that immediately 😤
options.why: Playful, but it shuts down a warm moment.

options.text: NO 😂 The day we got lost looking for that beach! Best holiday ever. We should go back.
options.why: You enjoy the memory together and dream about the future.

steps.body: Share a favourite memory with your partner today, and ask for theirs.
